analysis.title: "For Every $1 Bought, There Is $10 To Sell": Deutsche Warns The "AI Dollar" Is Here
key_insights: Deutsche Bank FX research head George Saravelos argues the dollar's risk-off properties cannot be taken for granted in an AI-driven tech correction. Over the last two weeks, sharp tech sell-offs and dollar sell-offs have occurred together.

Nasdaq 100 constituents lost more than $1.2 trillion in market cap in October. Amazon and Intel disappointed with results overnight. On Oct 15, stocks and the dollar fell together as the tech rout deepened.
Foreign equity inflows now finance the entire US current account deficit, which has rarely happened. Market concentration is at a record, with the top 10 S&P names at roughly 40% of the index.

Deutsche estimates roughly 90% of the $20+ trillion of US equities owned by foreigners reflects price appreciation rather than underlying buying. For every $1 of US equities bought, roughly $10 are now owned.

For a decade, US stocks and the dollar were negatively correlated, so a falling stock market was cushioned by a rising dollar. This gave foreign investors an incentive to hold US equity exposure unhedged.

Deutsche cites empirical evidence that the dollar-equity correlation turns positive when the equity shock originates in the US. The dollar then adds to equity losses and pushes investors to hedge more of their US assets, as around Liberation Day (April 2025).

State Street's Michael Metcalfe told Reuters on Oct 15 that foreign investors' hedge ratios on US positions were below 15%, down from about 25% in April. He added that a major equity rout could swing it around again.

Confirmation signal: if the 'USD down, equity down' dynamic is real, US real yields should fall alongside equities. Deutsche argues the 'rates higher, equities higher' move this year was driven by rising capex expectations, so a joint drop in real yields and equities would mean those expectations are being cut.

10Y yields posted their biggest daily drop in over a year on Oct 15 as chip stocks sold off. Microsoft launched a 10-part dollar high-grade bond deal on Oct 29, and the article's tracker counted $3.8 trillion of hyperscaler off-balance sheet liabilities as of Sept 30.
Saravelos says risks to the dollar are a lot more two-sided than the market has priced over the last few weeks. He states he is not expressing an opinion on the outlook of the AI ecosystem.

sector_views.rationale: The note discusses an ongoing AI-driven tech rout and the risk of further US-originated unwinding. It does not issue a formal sector rating.

earnings_insights: Amazon and Intel reported disappointing results overnight (reported around Oct 29-30, 2026), per the article. Alphabet is also cited as having disappointed. No EPS or revenue figures are given.

risk_factors: A US-originated equity shock could turn the dollar-equity correlation positive, so the dollar adds to losses instead of cushioning them.
Foreign investors could raise hedge ratios on US assets, creating dollar selling pressure.
Foreign holders of US equities are mostly sitting on price gains, which could be sold if tech continues to fall.
Continued hyperscaler debt issuance (Microsoft's 10-part bond deal, $3.8 trillion of off-balance sheet liabilities) adds to AI-related financing risk.
Top 10 S&P names at roughly 40% of the index increases index sensitivity to a few stocks.
vol_and_positioning: Foreign investors' hedge ratios on US equity positions are below 15%, down from about 25% in April (State Street).
Foreign holdings of US equities are described as unhedged and concentrated in a handful of megacaps, with roughly $18 trillion of mark-to-market gains by the article's napkin math.
The article's own view is that the market still treats the dollar as the default hedge for a tech crash and that positioning reflects this.
geopolitical: The article refers back to the April 2025 'Liberation Day' episode as a precedent for a simultaneous sell-off in all US assets.
The article mentions an oil shock in March 2026 that coincided with a dollar rally.
cross_bank_references: State Street's Michael Metcalfe told Reuters that foreign investors' hedge ratios on US positions were below 15%, down from about 25% in April.
Reuters noted on Oct 15 that stocks and the dollar slid together as the tech rout deepened.

tension_points.theme: dollar as safe haven in AI selloff
tension_points.bull_case: The market treats the dollar as the default hedge for a tech crash. For a decade, a falling US stock market came with a rising dollar, which cushioned foreign investors' losses.
tension_points.bear_case: When the equity shock is US-centric, the dollar-equity correlation turns positive, so the dollar adds to equity losses. Foreign holders are barely hedged and sit on large paper gains, so hedging shifts could add selling pressure.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A simultaneous drop in US real yields and equities would confirm the bear case. The dollar rallying during tech sell-offs would undermine it.

theme_stances.key_argument: The dollar's risk-off properties cannot be taken for granted in an AI-driven correction in the market.
theme_stances.evidence: risks to the dollar are a lot more two-sided than the market has been pricing
